answer: A tradition I love in my country is the celebration of Pohela Boishakh, the Bengali New Year. It takes place in mid-April and marks the beginning of the year according to our traditional calendar. It is a public holiday, so almost everyone is free to join in, whatever their background. On this day, people dress in traditional clothes, usually red and white, and the streets come alive with colourful processions, music and fairs. In Sirajganj, there is a big fair, or mela, where you can buy clay toys, handmade crafts and sweets, and children walk around with their faces painted. Many families start the morning with panta bhat, which is soaked rice, served with fried hilsa fish. What I find so special is how it brings the entire community together in a spirit of joy and [[renewal]]. Families gather to share traditional food, and there is a wonderful sense of [[festivity]] everywhere. It is important because it celebrates our cultural identity and heritage, which I think is vital to preserve. Unlike religious festivals, it belongs to every Bengali, which makes it wonderfully [[inclusive]]. In an increasingly globalised world, traditions like this help [[keep our roots alive]]. Honestly, the atmosphere on that day is genuinely [[uplifting]], and it fills people with optimism for the year ahead. Every year I go to the fair with my younger sister, and even though we buy the same sweets and wander past the same stalls, it never loses its charm. I think it is a beautiful example of how a shared tradition can strengthen a whole community's sense of belonging.

followUps.q: Has the way people celebrate it changed?
followUps.answer: Somewhat. It has become more commercial, with shops running special offers and people posting endless photos online. But the heart of it, dressing up and spending the day together outdoors, has stayed the same.

followUps.q: Do young people still care about this tradition?
followUps.answer: Very much, in my experience. If anything, young people are the most enthusiastic, because it is colourful, joyful and a chance to [[show off]] traditional outfits with friends.
